title: Fractional Indices

findings.finding: Simplifying even roots of algebraic powers requires an absolute-value distinction that the preceding teaching never explains.
findings.breakdown: Mechanical multiplication of exponents gives y for (y²)^(1/2), which is wrong when y is negative. The instruction that absolute value may be needed names the notation without teaching its meaning or use.
findings.checked: p3-q1 investigates squaring a square root, the reverse operation. p6-q9 addresses negative radicands. p8-q13-i introduces no explanatory contrast, and its answer is not teaching. p14-example-left explicitly restricts its variables to non-negative values; the later guided prompts do not explain unrestricted variables.
findings.assumptions: Variables are unrestricted unless stated otherwise. No calculator assumption is needed.

repair.proposal: Before p8-q13-i, add: 'A square root gives the non-negative root. If y = −3, √(y²) = √9 = 3, not −3. Therefore √(y²) = |y|, where |y| is the distance of y from zero. If y ≥ 0, this equals y.' Qualify the p14 key idea: 'When simplifying even roots, retain the non-negative result.'

findings.doneWhen: Students see the numerical contrast and the meaning of absolute value before its first required use, and the later key idea preserves that distinction.

findings.finding: The opening does not rehearse the negative-index reciprocal rule used in the numerical demonstration at p7-q12-a.
findings.breakdown: Students must retrieve the reciprocal operation while combining it with the newly introduced root interpretation.
findings.checked: The opening investigations rehearse powers of powers and roots. No preceding item retrieves negative indices before p7-q12-a demonstrates their combination with fractional indices.
findings.assumptions: Negative integer indices are prior learning from the separate course booklets. The targeted demonstration explicitly excludes calculators.

repair.proposal: Add a short opening review: '(a) Write 5^(−2) using positive indices. (b) Write (2/3)^(−3) using positive indices. (c) Evaluate 4^(−1).' Answers: 1/5², (3/2)³, 1/4. Keep the review within one page.

findings.doneWhen: Students retrieve the reciprocal rule before combining it with fractional indices.

findings.finding: p13-q6-d repeats the complete evaluation task 16^(5/4) from p12-q4-d.
findings.breakdown: Both parts require the same numerical evaluation without a calculator, with no explicit retrieval or comparison purpose.
findings.checked: The expression and substantive instructions match. The other proposed pair, p12-q5-i and p13-q6-a, has different task instructions: expressing in surd form or as a rational number versus evaluating without a calculator, so it is excluded from this finding.
findings.assumptions: No additional instructional purpose for the unchanged evaluation is stated.

repair.proposal: Replace p13-q6-d with 81^(5/4), retaining the instruction to evaluate without a calculator. Answer: 243.

findings.doneWhen: The later part retains its exponent structure with different numerical givens.

findings.finding: Connect numerical fractional powers with products involving opposite and related exponents.
findings.breakdown: The follow-up links evaluation to the same-base product law using the existing base 64.
findings.checked: The product law is practised in p8-q13 and p8-q14; general fractional powers and negative powers are available by this topic. The proposed answers are 1, 64 and 4.
findings.assumptions: These are optional follow-up parts completed without a calculator.
findings.doneWhen: The optional parts connect numerical evaluation with adding fractional exponents.

findings.finding: The opening example combines applying a power to every factor with multiplying nested exponents, without an opening rehearsal of that combination.
findings.breakdown: The step from (x^5y^3)^(1/2) to x^(5/2)y^(3/2) requires both laws together. Failure to distribute the outer power leaves one factor unchanged.
findings.checked: p3-q1 and p3-q2 rehearse powers of powers. The immediately preceding topic teaches root conversions, same-base products and reciprocal powers, but does not rehearse applying an outer power to every factor of a product.
findings.assumptions: Integer index laws are prior learning. No calculator is needed.

repair.proposal: Before p14-key-ideas-block, add: 'Simplify using index laws: (a) (x³)²; (b) (x²y³)²; (c) (2a³b)².' Answers: x⁶, x⁴y⁶, 4a⁶b². Keep the review within one page.

findings.doneWhen: Students rehearse applying an outer power to every factor and multiplying nested exponents before their combined fractional-index use.

findings.finding: Extend the existing numerical products by connecting an outside multiplier with the resulting exponent.
findings.breakdown: Students connect multiplication by the base with increasing its exponent by one.
findings.checked: Part h divided by part f gives 9. Also, 81√3 = 3^(9/2), and multiplying 3^(3/2) by 3 gives 3^(5/2). All required methods precede this question.
findings.assumptions: These are optional follow-up parts using positive numerical bases.

repair.proposal: After p18-q10-h, add: '(i) Divide the expression in part h by the expression in part f.' Answer: 9. '(j) Write 81√3 as a single power of 3.' Answer: 3^(9/2). '(k) Explain why multiplying 3√3 by 3 increases its exponent by 1 when written as a power of 3.' Answer: 3^(3/2) × 3¹ = 3^(5/2), because same-base multiplication adds exponents.

findings.doneWhen: The optional parts connect the existing numerical expressions with the product law.

findings.finding: The topic has no opening review of the numerical power recognition, bracket expansion and linear-equation solving combined in its worked examples.
findings.breakdown: Students must recognise common powers, expand an exponent and solve the resulting linear equation while learning the matching-bases method.
findings.checked: Earlier topics supply index laws and root conversions. Numerical powers occur in the preceding exercise, but the examples combine this recognition with separate algebraic methods, so the combined-method review exception applies. Bracket expansion and linear-equation solving are not rehearsed there.
findings.assumptions: These are prior skills from the listed course booklets. No calculator is needed for the proposed review.

repair.proposal: Before p21-information-block, add: '(a) Complete 25 = 5^□ and 125 = 5^□. (b) Complete 9 = 3^□ and 27 = 3^□. (c) Expand 2(2x−1). (d) Solve 2x = 3 and 4x−2 = 3.' Answers: (a) 2, 3; (b) 2, 3; (c) 4x−2; (d) x = 3/2, x = 5/4. Keep the review within one page.

findings.doneWhen: Students retrieve the numerical and algebraic steps before combining them in exponential equations.

findings.finding: p23-q5-d repeats the complete student task 27^(x+3) = 9^(2x) from p21-guided-2b.
findings.breakdown: The later part repeats the same givens and required operations without an explicit retrieval or comparison purpose.
findings.checked: The guided-practice prompt and later practice prompt are unchanged whole tasks. Neither contains an additional mathematical demand.
findings.assumptions: Guided practice is a student task; no separate purpose for its exact repetition is stated.
findings.doneWhen: The later part retains binomial exponents and unknowns on both sides with different givens.

findings.finding: The final simultaneous system abruptly requires solving for exponential quantities before matching exponents.
findings.breakdown: Earlier parts first turn each equation into a linear equation in the original variables. Part d instead introduces sums of powers and shifted exponents, requiring students to recognise two exponential quantities as the linear unknowns.
findings.checked: p27-q15-a through c all permit matching exponents first. Earlier products and quotients do not bridge the change to sums. Although d closes the exercise, the preceding parts do not build the changed first step, and no later bridge is available.
findings.assumptions: Ordinary simultaneous linear equations are prior knowledge.

repair.proposal: Add to p27-q15-d: 'Let U = 2^a and V = 3^b. Rewrite the system using U and V, noting that 2^(a+1) = 2U and 3^(b+1) = 3V. Find U and V first, then a and b.'

findings.doneWhen: Students have a route to U+V = 17 and 2U−3V = −11, giving U = 8, V = 9, a = 3 and b = 2.

findings.finding: The worked examples combine several index laws and ordinary common-factor extraction without an opening review.
findings.breakdown: Students must distribute powers, combine nested and same-base powers, and retain a residual 1 when extracting a common factor. Weak recall obstructs the new factorisation application.
findings.checked: The preceding topic practises several index laws, but the new examples combine methods from earlier topics with algebraic common-factor extraction. The combined-method exception therefore applies. p29-teaching announces extraction but does not rehearse the underlying algebraic skill.
findings.assumptions: Index laws and ordinary algebraic factorisation are prior learning. No calculator is needed.

repair.proposal: Before p28-information-block, add: 'Simplify (a) 2 × 2^n, (b) (3²)^n, (c) (2 × 5)^n. Factorise by taking out the common pronumeral: (d) y+yz, (e) u²+uv.' Answers: 2^(n+1), 3^(2n), 2^n × 5^n, y(1+z), u(u+v). Keep the review within one page.

findings.doneWhen: Students retrieve the combined index laws and common-factor extraction, including the residual 1.

findings.finding: Parts l and m repeat the complete tasks in h and i respectively.
findings.breakdown: The later pair repeats identical expressions under the same instruction without an explicit retrieval or comparison purpose.
findings.checked: Both pairs have unchanged numerators, denominators, exponents and instructions. The proposed replacements preserve the factorisation and cancellation structures.
findings.assumptions: Expressions are considered where their original denominators are non-zero.

repair.proposal: Replace l with (5^n+5^(n+2))/(5^(n−1)+5^(n+1)), answer 5. Replace m with (3^(2n)−3^(n−1))/(3^n−3^(−1)), answer 3^n, where the original denominator is non-zero (n ≠ −1 for real n).

findings.doneWhen: Both later copies use different numbers while retaining their original mathematical structures.

findings.finding: The final equation requires recognising and solving a quadratic in an exponential expression, a variant not modelled earlier.
findings.breakdown: Students must recognise 4^x as (2^x)², factorise in the quantity 2^x, reject a negative exponential value and then return to x. The taught matching-exponents procedure does not supply this route.
findings.checked: p21-information names a quadratic exponential equation but teaches only matching bases. Its examples and p33-q9-a and b do not model quadratic substitution or the positivity check. Closing the exercise does not supply the missing method.
findings.assumptions: Ordinary quadratic factorisation is prior learning; its application to an exponential quantity is new here.

repair.proposal: Before p33-q9-c, model: 'Solve 9^x−2 × 3^x−3 = 0. Since 9^x = (3^x)², let t = 3^x. Then t²−2t−3 = (t−3)(t+1) = 0, so t = 3 or −1. Since 3^x > 0, reject −1. Thus 3^x = 3 and x = 1.'

findings.doneWhen: Students see quadratic recognition, factorisation, the positivity check and the return to an exponential equation before the required task.

findings.finding: Extend the existing sum with a run varying only the exponent gap.
findings.breakdown: The coefficient changes with the exponent gap while the base and extracted factor remain fixed.
findings.checked: Together with the existing gap-one expression, the additions form a four-question run. Their coefficients are 4, 10, 28 and 82. The unpatterned subtraction gives 26 × 3^n. The methods are modelled in p29.
findings.assumptions: Use new subpart labels so existing part labels remain distinct.

repair.proposal: Immediately after p31-q3-g, under the existing factorisation instruction, add the single instruction 'Predict the coefficient before factorising.' Add 3^n+3^(n+2), answer 10 × 3^n; 3^n+3^(n+3), answer 28 × 3^n; and 3^n+3^(n+4), answer 82 × 3^n. Follow with 3^(n+3)−3^n, answer 26 × 3^n.

findings.doneWhen: The run varies the exponent gap while holding the base, addition and common factor fixed, followed by an unpatterned question.

protectedGroups.observation: Taking the power before or after the square root gives the same fractional-index representation.
protectedGroups.varies: Whether the fifth power is inside or outside the root.
protectedGroups.invariant: Base m, square root and fifth power.

protectedGroups.observation: The two orders of applying the fourth root and cube agree.
protectedGroups.varies: Placement of the cube relative to the radical.
protectedGroups.invariant: Base 10, fourth root and cube.

protectedGroups.observation: The denominator selects the root and the numerator selects the power.
protectedGroups.varies: First the root index, then the numerator.
protectedGroups.invariant: Base 8.

protectedGroups.observation: Scaling a base by 1000 scales its cube root by 10 and the square of that cube root by 100; the recurrence of p12-q4-a within this comparison has an instructional purpose.
protectedGroups.varies: Base 27 versus 27000, repeated for exponents 1/3 and 2/3.
protectedGroups.invariant: Cube-root denominator and the paired base relationship.

protectedGroups.observation: Changing only the exponent's sign takes the reciprocal of the result.
protectedGroups.varies: Positive versus negative exponent.
protectedGroups.invariant: Base 8/27 and exponent magnitude 1/3.

protectedGroups.observation: The scope of the fractional exponent determines which parts of a quotient are rooted.

protectedGroups.invariant: Numbers 16 and 9 and exponent 1/4.

protectedGroups.invariant: The base 64.

protectedGroups.invariant: The evaluated value 2.

protectedGroups.varies: Exponent placement, grouping, sign and root order.
protectedGroups.invariant: The numerical factor 64 and variable x.

protectedGroups.observation: Exchanging the two fractional exponents preserves the resulting exponent on x while changing the power applied to 64.
protectedGroups.varies: Which of 1/2 and 1/3 is the inner exponent and which is the outer exponent.

protectedGroups.varies: Grouping around 3x.
